shots.text: The British archaeologist Bernard Fagg collected the finds, and gave them a name: the Nok culture.
shots.desc: generic mid-century archive shelves with closed boxes, soft window light, no desk, no person, no papers with writing

shots.text: Many of his pieces came from tin-mine gravels, moved from where they had first lain.
shots.desc: wet alluvial gravels in an old tin-mine cutting, overcast

shots.text: According to Fagg's later account, as retold in Archaeology magazine, a terracotta head had been used on a scarecrow in a yam field.
shots.desc: yam mounds in a field, a scarecrow silhouette against sky, head not shown

shots.text: It was brought to him in Jos.
shots.desc: 1940s town street on a plateau, late afternoon, no faces

shots.text: It is known as the Jemaa head, after the village where it was found.
shots.desc: rural village edge, granite boulders, evening smoke

shots.text: In the wake of Fagg's publications, Nok pieces flooded the international art market.
shots.desc: wooden crates stacked in a dim warehouse, straw packing

shots.text: Sites were dug out for sale, and the record of where things lay was lost.
shots.desc: freshly dug pits in red earth at night, torchlight, no people

shots.text: Later, archaeologists from Goethe University Frankfurt went looking.
shots.desc: 4x4 on a dirt track through the plateau, dust

shots.text: All of the team's first thirty sites had been looted.
shots.desc: field of abandoned looters' pits, spoil heaps, grass regrowing
